newsitem.title: IRAQ: Kurdish guerrillas dig in against Iraqi troops.
newsitem.headline: Kurdish guerrillas dig in against Iraqi troops.

text.p: Barricades along a mountain road between the town of Chamchamal and Bazian pass represent the last line of defence for Kurdish rebels facing what they say are thousands of Iraqi troops backed by tanks and artillery.
Guerrillas of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) dug trenches by the side of the road and vowed to fight to the death to defend their stronghold Sulaimaniya, 60 km (40 miles) to the east.
The earthworks, three metres (10 feet) high in places, seal off the road linking Sulaimaniya to the oil city of Kirkuk with just a narrow passage for cars or small armoured vehicles.
PUK commanders say they can field about 1,000 experienced guerrillas, with arms ranging from automatic rifles to rocket-propelled grenades and light cannon.

Arrayed against them, they say, are thousands of troops from President Saddam Hussein's army -- backed by artillery and more than 120 tanks -- newly allied with the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) militia.
"We will stay and fight until the last drop of our blood flows away," said one PUK guerrilla, hard at work on the city's forward defensive line.

On August 31, Iraqi forces intervened on behalf of the KDP to oust the PUK from the city of Arbil, capital of the predominantly-Kurdish north. That forced PUK leader Jalal Talabani to regroup in and around Sulaimaniya.
The battle for Arbil marked a turning point in the 30-year-old PUK-KDP feud, setting up what Western aid workers and diplomat expect to be a final showdown.
Chamchamal, on the eastern edge of the Bani Makan hills, marks the closest approach of a joint Iraq-Kurdish force to Sulaimaniya, the last major settlement in PUK hands.

"The enemy is only four km (2.5 miles) from our town and prefers to bombard at night to scare the residents. Half our population fled to Sulaimaniya," said Salah Mohammad, militia commander for the town that once held 20,000.
"We have more than 1,000 fighters, ready to die for their homeland and freedom, in and around the town," he told Reuters.

The road from Sulaimaniya to Chamchamal is pocked with craters. PUK guerrillas man checkpoints and dig trenches. Only scattered vehicles hazard the trip, all dabbed with mud in an attempt to blend in with the hills beyond.
"Saddam's soldiers watch the main road and can see the colours of the cars and hit them with rockets," said Hemin Vahap, an 18-year-old PUK guerrilla. "That's why we paint our vehicles with mud."
The PUK has set up its defence headquarters at the settlement of Teke, near the Bazian pass.
"This is the most important position of our resistance because it is the closest point to Sulaimaniya," said Osman, a guerrilla commander.
"We will never let them pass through Chamchamal. When they begin shelling, we answer back at once," he said.

In Sulaimaniya, nervous residents and refugees fleeing the fighting grasp at any piece of news, broadcast from loudspeakers nailed to the fronts of PUK party buildings. Emotions rise and fall with each bulletin.
The bodies of dead PUK fighters are led through the streets in green-draped coffins, crowds of mourners wailing beside them.
"We will resist and fight until we all die, because we do not want our city destroyed and our children killed by Saddam," said Sallah Shabab, father of 10.
"America will stop Saddam and not permit another massacre," said Shabab, 35.
Sulaimaniya residents have largely pinned their hopes on Washington, which sent two volleys of cruise missiles slamming into southern Iraq in retaliation for Saddam's push into the Kurdish north.
PUK television, in a bid to boost morale, has broadcast archive footage of U.S. fighter-bombers attacking Baghdad in the 1991 Gulf War. Heroic songs also fill the airwaves.
Kurdistan Communist Party supporters staged a big demonstration against Saddam and his new partner, Massoud Barzani of the KDP, in the central square.

The news from the front has also unsettled prices in the Sulaimaniya market. Petrol prices tripled on first word of Iraqi shelling of Chamchamal to six dinars per litre, and then doubled again on Saturday to 12 dinars.
The U.S. dollar climbed to 28 dinars from 24.5 dinars on Thursday, but fell back to 26 dinars at the weekend.
